source.title: Pole solutions in the case of problems of flame front propagation and Saffman-Teylor "finger" formation without surface tension: open problems and possible ways of their solutions

accepted.question_text: For zero-surface-tension Saffman-Taylor/Laplacian growth in a channel represented by pole solutions, when one tries to make the zero-surface-tension dynamics reproduce the effects of vanishingly small surface tension by continually adding new remote poles, should the permanent source of those new poles be modeled as external noise, or as an infinite number of poles already present in the initial condition? In particular, which of those two mechanisms is the preferred explanation in the channel Laplacian-growth setting?
accepted.context_brief: Source of remote poles in channel Laplacian growth

evidence.quote: Summing up, it is possible to tell, that for identity of the results with and without surface tension it is necessary to introduce a permanent source of the new remote poles: it may be either external noise or infinite number of poles in an initial condition. What from these methods is preferred it is a open question yet. In the case of flame front propagation it was shown [7], that external noise is necessary for an explanation of flame front velocity increase with the sizes of system: the infinite number of poles in an initial condition can not give this result. It is interesting to know, what is situation in the channel Laplacian growth.

accepted.question_text: For finite-pole pole solutions of zero-surface-tension channel Laplacian growth, what are the exact necessary conditions that classify an initial pole configuration as allowed, meaning that it does not approach a finite-time singularity, rather than as an initial configuration that leads to a finite-time singularity?
accepted.context_brief: Allowed versus singular initial pole conditions

evidence.quote: In our teamwork with Mark Mineev-Weinstein [5] it was shown, that for finite number of poles at almost all allowed (in the sense of not approaching to finite time singularities) initial conditions, except for small number of some degenerated initial conditions, they have asymptotic as some "finger" with any possible thickness.
Exact necessary conditions, whether defining the initial pole condition as "allowed", i.e. singular, is still a open problem.

accepted.question_text: For the general pole solution in zero-surface-tension Saffman-Taylor channel growth, let the real parameter α be the sum of the complex pole parameters α_i, and let the asymptotic finger thickness be 1 − α/2, so that α = 1 corresponds to a finger of half the channel width and 0 < α < 2 corresponds to physically possible finger thicknesses between 0 and 1. As a function of α in the interval 0 < α < 2, what fraction of all possible initial pole configurations with that α are allowed rather than singular, and does this α-dependent distribution support selection of the half-width finger as the most probable asymptotic outcome?
accepted.context_brief: Distribution of allowed initial conditions over α

evidence.quote: The general pole solution (5) in work [3] is characterized by the real parameter α being the sum of the complex parameters αi for poles. Thickness of the asymptotic finger is simple function of α: (Thickness = 1 − α/2). The value (α = 1) corresponds to thickness 1/2. As far as possible thickness of the "finger" is between 0 and 1, possible α value is in an interval between 0 and 2: (0 < α < 2).

How number of these "allowed" initial pole conditions (to be exact speaking, their percent from the full number of the possible initial pole conditions corresponding to the given real value α) is distributed inside of this interval?

accepted.question_text: Can one give a strict proof, for zero-surface-tension Saffman-Taylor channel growth in the pole-solution formulation, that the exclusion of finite-time-singular initial pole configurations together with continual introduction of new poles selects a single finger of half the channel width as the privileged or most probable asymptotic state?
accepted.context_brief: Strict proof of half-width finger selection

evidence.quote: It does not mean, nevertheless, that privileged role of "finger" with thickness 1/2 cannot be proved in the case of surface tension absence, but means only that such the proof are not given in [3]. Let us try to give these correct arguments here.
Source of new poles results to the drift of finger thickness, but this thickness drift is closed to the most probable and average size equal to 1/2!
These given arguments are not, certainly, the strict proof, but only specifies a way to it. The inquisitive reader is invited to make and publish it.

accepted.question_text: For cylindrical flame-front propagation governed by the flame-front motion equation in the absence of explicit external noise, with only numerical noise present in simulations, does the flame-front velocity eventually saturate, or does it continue to accelerate indefinitely?
accepted.context_brief: Velocity saturation in cylindrical flame-front propagation

evidence.quote: For a cylindrical case of the flame front propagation problem at absence of noise (only numerical noise) (look [7] and the bibliography there) by Sivashinsky with help of numerical methods it was shown, that the flame front is continuously accelerated. During all this account time it is not visible any attributes of saturation. To increase time of the account is a difficult task. Hence, absence or presence of velocity saturation in a cylindrical case, as consequence of the flame front motion equation it is still a open problem yet.

accepted.question_text: In numerical simulations of cylindrical flame-front propagation, does adding explicit Gaussian noise produce a flame-front velocity saturation point, and how does the position or behavior of that saturation point depend on the Gaussian-noise amplitude when extrapolated toward small numerical noise?
accepted.context_brief: Gaussian-noise saturation-point study for cylindrical flames

evidence.quote: Introduction obvious Gaussian noise results to appearance of a point of saturation and its removal from the origin of coordinates with decreasing of noise amplitude, allowing extrapolating results on small numerical noise. ( Fig. 2.6 in [7]) Hence, introducing of Gaussian noise in numerical calculation also for a cylindrical case can again results to appearance of a saturation point and will allow to investigate its behavior as function of noise amplitude by extrapolating results on small numerical noise. The Inquisitive Reader loved by me is invited again to make it and to publish the received interesting results.
